teenKit.tldr: Cells don't always die politely; sometimes they suffer a catastrophic, iron-fueled chemical blaze called ferroptosis where rogue waves of oxidation rip through their outer walls. Biology textbooks missed this brutal process for decades, focusing instead on tidy, self-dismantling cell death.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how cells burn from the inside out gives scientists the ultimate weapon to fight neurodegenerative diseases and stop rogue cancer cells in their tracks.
keyTakeaways: Ferroptosis is a newly discovered, highly violent form of cell death driven by iron and runaway lipid peroxidation rather than quiet, orderly aging.
Instead of just packing their bags, cells under attack will perform frantic molecular amputations, slicing off burning pieces of their own anatomy to survive.
At an atomic scale of just one angstrom, the inside of a living cell transforms from a peaceful microscopic bubble into a raging chemical war zone.

vocab.meaning: A newly uncovered type of regulated cell death caused by iron-dependent chemical fires that destroy cell membranes.
